questions.q: What is this lesson's purpose, per its own framing?
options: A map/orientation before the deep dives ahead, not something to memorize in detail
A complete, exhaustive technical comparison replacing the need for later chapters
A ranking of which platform is objectively the best
A tutorial for installing all four platforms
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames itself as orienting context to refer back to, not a deep technical dive.

questions.q: What genuinely interesting corporate wrinkle does this lesson flag about MySQL?
options: Oracle Corporation actually owns MySQL today, though this doesn't make them the same product or architecture
MySQL is owned by Microsoft
MySQL has never had any commercial ownership
MySQL and PostgreSQL are made by the same company
questions.explain: Oracle Corporation acquired MySQL via its acquisition of Sun Microsystems — a real, worth-knowing fact that doesn't imply architectural similarity.

questions.q: Why does this lesson caution that 'open source' doesn't mean 'free of all cost'?
options: Running MySQL or PostgreSQL at scale still costs money in infrastructure, support contracts, and DBA time
Open source databases are illegal to use commercially
Open source software always requires a paid license eventually
There is no real cost difference between any of the four platforms
questions.explain: Open source removes the per-core software license line item specifically, not all real-world costs.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about 'typical use case' labels like 'Oracle for enterprise' or 'PostgreSQL for new projects'?
options: They describe tendencies, not rules — you'll find exceptions like Oracle running web apps or PostgreSQL running core finance systems
They are strict, universal rules with no exceptions
Typical use case has no bearing on real-world deployments
Every company must follow these use-case assignments exactly
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against treating the table as a rigid rule rather than general orientation.

questions.q: Which two factors does this lesson identify as connecting back to Lesson 2's reasons companies end up running multiple database platforms?
options: Licensing pressure and use-case fit
Server hostname conventions and time zone settings
The number of employees at a company
Whether a company uses cloud or on-premises infrastructure exclusively
questions.explain: The lesson ties licensing model and typical use case directly back to real, practical reasons for multi-platform environments.
